Recent work supports separating predictive history use from sensitivity to sequence edits. “Measuring Recency Bias” (2024) introduces a recency metric and reports accuracy improvements after mitigating excessive recent-item emphasis; this does not establish that recency dependence is inherently undesirable. A 2026 benchmark study finds pairwise history models outperform SASRec/eSASRec reproductions on four of five datasets, motivating last-item Markov, additive item-transition, and recency-weighted reference models before attributing gains to higher-order sequence reasoning. [Recency study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722), [benchmark study](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling).

Counterfactual explanation methods offer useful intervention machinery: a 2025 genetic-algorithm approach searches for minimal history changes, while TRACE (2026) targets bringing specified items into or pushing them out of recommendations, measuring validity and edit distance. These assess model behavior under edits; they do not establish causal user preferences. [2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606), [TRACE](https://github.com/devUuung/TRACE).

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: freeze each user’s target and candidate set; compare paired edits matched by replacement count and source-item popularity. Separate identity substitutions at fixed positions, permutations preserving the item multiset and occupied positions, and repetition changes holding length and latest item fixed. Compare deletion with in-place replacement to expose compaction effects; test padding/position shifts separately while preserving valid-item order. Include unchanged-input controls, multiple random draws, and popularity, last-item, and additive-history baselines. Report paired target-score/rank changes and validation HR@10 with uncertainty. Treat these as proposed controls informed by the literature, rather than an established causal identification protocol.
